power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = .073", "P = .71"), Sentence = c("Arithmetic mean payments were $163,087 and $131,837, respectively, with a difference of +$31,250 (95% CI -$3,006 to +$65,506; P = .073).", "The pooled arithmetic mean was $136,979 (SD $139,961), compared with $131,837 (SD $129,242), with a difference of +$5,142 (95% CI -$22,362 to +$32,646; P = .71)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background: Medicare payment patterns among neurosurgeons with private equity connections remain poorly characterized.
We compared annual professional payments by connection type.
Methods: In this retrospective cross-sectional study, public Medicare provider summaries for 2013-2024 were linked to dated affiliation and investment records.
The primary comparison included 69 practice or management-services organization-connected surgeons and 4,016 comparison surgeons.
Connected surgeons contributed index-year payments; comparison surgeons contributed averages over eligible years.
Welch comparisons of log payments estimated geometric mean ratios.
Supporting analyses examined dollar differences, state-year standardization, beneficiary age/risk balance, 35 hospital-operator surgeons, and longitudinal trajectories.
Payments were expressed in 2024 US dollars.
Results: The primary geometric mean ratio was 1.38 (95% confidence interval 1.

Private equity (PE) investment has become an increasingly visible feature of physician practice organization, including surgical specialties. [10] Practices may join investor-backed platforms through direct acquisition, management-services arrangements, or other economic relationships.
text.formatted: Private equity (PE) investment has become an increasingly visible feature of physician practice organization, including surgical specialties. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[10]</ref> Practices may join investor-backed platforms through direct acquisition, management-services arrangements, or other economic relationships.

text.text: These arrangements can affect referral patterns and how clinical services are scheduled and delivered.

Studies in other procedural specialties have linked PE involvement to differences in spending and utilization, although their findings vary by specialty and outcome. [2, 5, 8, 11] For neurological surgery, comparing the professional activity of surgeons in investor-linked practices with that of other surgeons can inform discussions of practice organization and consolidation.
text.formatted: Studies in other procedural specialties have linked PE involvement to differences in spending and utilization, although their findings vary by specialty and outcome. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">11]</ref> For neurological surgery, comparing the professional activity of surgeons in investor-linked practices with that of other surgeons can inform discussions of practice organization and consolidation.

text.text: The neurosurgical literature has examined the future of private practice and the implications of PE investment. [1] Recent conference abstracts have also described PE-backed neurosurgical care and consolidation in spine ambulatory surgery centers. [6, 7] Physician-level payment comparisons extend this transaction-focused literature by examining the professional activity of neurosurgeons with documented investment connections.
text.formatted: The neurosurgical literature has examined the future of private practice and the implications of PE investment. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> Recent conference abstracts have also described PE-backed neurosurgical care and consolidation in spine ambulatory surgery centers. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">7]</ref> Physician-level payment comparisons extend this transaction-focused literature by examining the professional activity of neurosurgeons with documented investment connections.

text.text: A practice or management-services organization (MSO) relationship is particularly relevant to this question because it links investment to the organization of physician services.
Surgeons employed by investor-owned hospital systems may have different payment patterns from those in PE-backed physician practices.

Medicare provider summaries offer a consistent national source of annual professional payments and service measures. [3] These payments reflect the volume and composition of reimbursed care, rather than physician compensation alone.
text.formatted: Medicare provider summaries offer a consistent national source of annual professional payments and service measures. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[3]</ref> These payments reflect the volume and composition of reimbursed care, rather than physician compensation alone.

text.text: Traditional Medicare rates generally follow an administered fee schedule, while annual provider payments can vary with beneficiary volume, service mix, geography, and billing.
We compared annual Medicare professional payments among neurosurgeons with documented PE-backed practice or practice-linked MSO connections and comparison surgeons without an identified connection.
The main comparison examined proportional payment differences using geometric means.
Supporting analyses examined absolute dollar differences, geographical and temporal composition, and payment trajectories around organizational investment.
Hospital-operator relationships and the pooled investmentconnected cohort were evaluated separately to place the practice/MSO findings in context.

We conducted a retrospective observational study using Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners provider summaries for 2013-2024. [3] The study was a descriptive physician-level cross-sectional comparison, centered on practice/MSO connections.
text.formatted: We conducted a retrospective observational study using Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners provider summaries for 2013-2024. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[3]</ref> The study was a descriptive physician-level cross-sectional comparison, centered on practice/MSO connections.

text.text: Connected surgeons contributed one index-year observation, and comparison surgeons contributed their mean payment over eligible years.
A supporting longitudinal analysis used annual records around the start of the organization's recorded investment window.
The connected index observations occurred in 2015 and 2018-2024 across 30 states and 52 state-year strata.
This study is reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guideline.
Potential PE-backed organizations were identified using PitchBook and targeted searches of public company announcements and investment-firm websites through October 2026.
Physician affiliations were established from dated practice rosters and archived records and linked to CMS data by National Provider Identifier (NPI).
One investigator reviewed the supporting evidence to confirm professional relationships and investment timing.
Dated CMS group-membership records and other professional-affiliation documents supplemented the roster review.
Supplementary Methods and Table S1 describe the classification and organization-specific analytical windows.
text.formatted: Supplementary Methods and Table <ref type="table">S1</ref> describe the classification and organization-specific analytical windows.

text.text: Inclusion required an individual CMS provider record classified as neurosurgery, a dated qualifying professional relationship, and an organizational investment link covering the dated observation.
Qualifying relationships included membership in a PE-backed practice, a practicelinked MSO arrangement, or employment in a hospital-operator professional group.
Documented minority equity investment qualified; hospital privileges alone and debt-only financing did not.
Unresolved relationships and observations outside the supported window were not included.
After duplicate removal, each surgeon's earliest eligible dated observation with same-year CMS presence defined the index year.
The main exposure group comprised 69 practice/MSO-connected surgeons.
A separate group of 35 hospital-operator professional-group surgeons provided a secondary comparison.
The latter category included LifePoint, Steward, and Quorum, encompassing both conventional PE sponsorship and investment-fund ownership following restructuring.
This broader employment category was analyzed separately from practice/MSO relationships.
BASS/Privia was classified through its practice-linked MSO and retained sponsor equity during the 2022 index observations; public listing alone was not an exclusion.
These definitions identify professional economic connections and do not imply that every practice was directly acquired.
Comparison surgeons were individual neurosurgeons with provider summaries in the connected cohort's state-year strata.
Physicians with known or unresolved professional PE connections in the screening inventory, and specified exact organizational matches, were excluded from the comparison pool across years.
The resulting pool contained 4,016 distinct physicians and 8,118 physician-years.
Connected and comparison NPIs did not overlap.
Comparisons were geographically and temporally restricted, rather than individually matched; the term comparison denotes no identified connection within the reviewed inventory.

The primary outcome was annual provider-wide Medicare professional payment, CMS Tot_Mdcr_Pymt_Amt, converted to 2024 US dollars using the annual all-items Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers. [13] Payments represent traditional Medicare fee-for-service activity attributed to the provider and exclude facility revenue, Medicare Advantage payments, and commercial insurance activity.
text.formatted: The primary outcome was annual provider-wide Medicare professional payment, CMS Tot_Mdcr_Pymt_Amt, converted to 2024 US dollars using the annual all-items Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[13]</ref> Payments represent traditional Medicare fee-for-service activity attributed to the provider and exclude facility revenue, Medicare Advantage payments, and commercial insurance activity.

text.text: Annual beneficiary counts and service units provided practice context.
Beneficiaries were distinct within physician-year, and service units were billed units rather than surgical cases.
Provider-level mean beneficiary age and risk score were used in a supporting balancing analysis.
Missing or suppressed values were not assigned zero; payment, age, and risk variables were complete in the cross-sectional analytical records.
The main analysis compared natural-log annual payments between practice/MSO-connected surgeons and comparison surgeons using a two-sided Welch t-test.

Practice/MSO connections identify the physician-practice investment exposure of interest, and the log scale summarizes proportional payment differences while reducing the influence of extreme dollar values in the right-skewed distribution.
Exponentiating the difference in mean log payments and its 95% confidence interval (CI) yielded the geometric mean ratio.
Each practice/MSO surgeon contributed an index-year payment; each comparison surgeon contributed the arithmetic mean of eligible annual payments before log transformation.
Physicians were weighted equally within the group.
Supporting analyses compared arithmetic mean payments with Welch CIs, allowing unequal group variances, and median payments with physician-level bootstrap CIs.
Mann-Whitney tests assessed distributional differences, not equality of medians specifically.
The same dollar and log comparisons were reported separately for hospital-operator connections and for the pooled 104surgeon connected cohort.
All estimates and P values were nominal, without multiplicity adjustment, and were interpreted together as descriptive observational comparisons.
State-year standardization weighted each within-stratum arithmetic mean difference by that stratum's share of connected surgeons, using the practice/MSO distribution for the practice/MSO estimate.

Relative-entropy weighting was applied separately to the practice/MSO and pooled cohorts, preserving each cohort's state-year totals while balancing mean provider-level beneficiary age and risk score.
Practice/MSO weighting estimated dollar differences and geometric mean ratios from annual payment records; the state-year-only log contrast used the same annual-record aggregation.
These weighted contrasts target a different composition from the main comparison of physician-level payment summaries.
Percentile CIs used 19,999 bootstrap draws for practice/MSO-balanced estimates and the state-year-only log ratio, and 4,999 for the other standardized, pooled-balanced, and median estimates.
Draws resampled physicians within each group, retained all eligible annual records and multiplicities, and refitted weights.
The practice/MSO annual-record bootstrap sampled 69 connected surgeons and the 3,294 comparison physicians contributing records in its 36 eligible state-year strata.
These crosssectional procedures assume independence between physicians and do not adjust for shared organizations.

The supporting longitudinal analysis included 50 practice/MSO surgeons and 20 hospitaloperator surgeons with at least one CMS record in the index state before organizational investment and at least one in the following two years.

A stacked difference-in-differences model used state-investment-year subexperiments, physician-by-subexperiment and year-bysubexperiment fixed effects, and comparison sample-share weights.[ 14] The investment year was excluded.
Standard errors were clustered by connected parent organization and by comparison physician, using a t reference with connected-organization clusters minus one degrees of freedom.
Dollar, log-payment, and event-study models characterized payment trajectories.

Sensitivity analyses stratified cross-sectional comparisons by provider-address Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes (1-3 metropolitan; 4-10 nonmetropolitan), omitted influential parent organizations, and excluded uncertain affiliation index years.

For practice/MSO longitudinal models, we used a restricted wild cluster bootstrap t CI (9,999 Webb six-point draws), omitted each parent in turn, removed surgeons above the 99th and 95th percentiles of preinvestment mean payment, and restricted the cohort to 46 surgeons with a preinvestment record matching their index ZIP code.
Hospital-operator DiD results were reported as point estimates because only three connected parent clusters were available.
Organizational investment dates, rather than verified individual acquisition dates, anchored the longitudinal models.
Detailed methods and results are in the supplement.
Analyses used Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5, and SciPy 1.17.0.
Two-sided P < .05 was the nominal significance threshold.
text.formatted: Two-sided P < .05 was the nominal significance threshold.

text.text: Institutional review board review was not required for this study, which used publicly available provider-level records and contained no individual patient clinical records.
The source inventory contained 10,474 candidate records: 3,046 accepted, 2,130 rejected, and 5,298 unresolved.
Removing 34 duplicate accepted records yielded 3,012 eligible dated professional observations representing 104 distinct connected surgeons (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Removing 34 duplicate accepted records yielded 3,012 eligible dated professional observations representing 104 distinct connected surgeons (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: These sourcerecord counts reflect documentary observations, not unique physicians.
The cohort comprised 69 practice/MSO surgeons across 20 parent-organization labels and 35 hospital-operator surgeons across three labels (Table 1).
text.formatted: The cohort comprised 69 practice/MSO surgeons across 20 parent-organization labels and 35 hospital-operator surgeons across three labels (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: LifePoint accounted for 27 hospital-operator surgeons, Steward for five, and Quorum for three.
Practice/MSO and comparison surgeons had mean beneficiary ages of 73.2 and 71.8 years and risk scores of 1.30 and 1.53, respectively.
Practice and MSO payment comparisons Practice/MSO-connected surgeons had geometric mean annual Medicare professional payments of $114,555, compared with $82,829 among comparison surgeons.
The geometric mean ratio was 1.38 (95% CI 1.11-1.72; P = .004), corresponding to 38% higher geometric mean payments (Table 2; Figure 2).
text.formatted: The geometric mean ratio was 1.38 (95% CI 1.11-1.72; P = .004), corresponding to 38% higher geometric mean payments (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: Arithmetic mean payments were $163,087 and $131,837, respectively, with a difference of +$31,250 (95% CI -$3,006 to +$65,506; P = .073).
Median payments were $117,101 and $98,094; the median difference was +$19,007 (bootstrap 95% CI -$5,406 to +$70,125; Table S2).
text.formatted: Median payments were $117,101 and $98,094; the median difference was +$19,007 (bootstrap 95% CI -$5,406 to +$70,125; Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: The practice/MSO state-year standardized arithmetic mean difference was +$32,204 (95% CI +$2,886 to +$65,372; Table 3).
text.formatted: The practice/MSO state-year standardized arithmetic mean difference was +$32,204 (95% CI +$2,886 to +$65,372; Table <ref type="table">3</ref>).

text.text: After age/risk balancing, the dollar difference was +$19,708 (95% CI -$10,419 to +$52,919) and the geometric mean ratio was 1.25 (95% CI 1.01-1.59).
The corresponding state-year-only log ratio was 1.31 (95% CI 1.07-1.60; Figure 2B).
text.formatted: The corresponding state-year-only log ratio was 1.31 (95% CI 1.07-1.60; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2B</ref>).

text.text: Findings persisted among metropolitan providers and after omitting influential parent organizations or uncertain index-year assignments (Tables S5-S9).
text.formatted: Findings persisted among metropolitan providers and after omitting influential parent organizations or uncertain index-year assignments (Tables <ref type="table">S5-S9</ref>).

text.text: Hospital-operator surgeons had lower payment levels, with a geometric mean ratio of 0.53 (95% CI 0.35-0.81) relative to comparison surgeons.
Their arithmetic mean payment was $85,508, with a difference of -$46,328 (95% CI -$88,708 to -$3,949; P = .033), and their median payment was $58,678.
The state-year standardized mean difference was -$50,464 (95% CI -$83,099 to -$8,807).
Pooling both connection types yielded a geometric mean ratio of 1.00 (95% CI 0.81-1.25).
The pooled arithmetic mean was $136,979 (SD $139,961), compared with $131,837 (SD $129,242), with a difference of +$5,142 (95% CI -$22,362 to +$32,646; P = .71).
The pooled state-year standardized difference was +$4,383 (95% CI -$20,531 to +$32,291); additional beneficiary age/risk balancing yielded -$4,900 (95% CI -$29,306 to +$22,584).
The pooled intervals included substantial differences in either direction.
Contextual state-year standardized annual beneficiary counts were 189.3 versus 186.3, and service units were 595.5 versus 554.7, among all connected and comparison surgeons, respectively.

Among the 50 practice/MSO surgeons eligible for longitudinal analysis, mean payments before and after organizational investment were $238,715 and $187,231, compared with $163,972 and $133,810 among comparison surgeons.
The model-based log-payment change was +16.9% (95% CI -0.3% to +37.2%).
The dollar change was -$15,727 per year (clustered 95% CI -$78,207 to +$46,753; wild cluster bootstrap 95% CI -$95,893 to +$35,191).
Removing the highest preinvestment biller changed the dollar estimate to +$8,556 (95% CI -$13,658 to +$30,770).
Parent-omission, upper-tail, and same-ZIP estimates are reported in Figure S1 and Tables S7 and S8.

text.text: The scale-dependent direction and influence of the upper tail limit interpretation of investment-related change.
Practice/MSO event-study estimates were imprecise.

Hospital-operator payments showed a differential change of -$30,848; the coefficient for four or more years before investment was +$43,790 (95% CI +$22,512 to +$65,069), providing evidence inconsistent with parallel trends (Figure 3; Tables S3 and S4).
text.formatted: Hospital-operator payments showed a differential change of -$30,848; the coefficient for four or more years before investment was +$43,790 (95% CI +$22,512 to +$65,069), providing evidence inconsistent with parallel trends (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>; Tables <ref type="table">S3</ref> and <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Neurosurgeons with documented PE-backed practice or practice-linked MSO connections had higher unadjusted geometric mean Medicare payments than comparison surgeons (ratio 1.38; 95% CI 1.11-1.72), while the age/risk-balanced ratio was 1.25 (95% CI 1.01-1.59), with a lower confidence bound close to unity.
The state-year standardized arithmetic mean difference was approximately $32,000.
The unstandardized arithmetic mean and median differences were also positive, although their CIs included zero.
Practice organization and payment profiles Practice/MSO connections correspond to the physician-practice investment relationships examined in other procedural specialties.
Direct acquisitions, minority equity investments, and practice-linked management arrangements can differ in control and operations.

The payment difference persisted among metropolitan providers and after omitting influential parent organizations, suggesting that broad rurality or a single large organization did not fully explain the association.
Provider-address RUCA codes do not describe patients' residential geography or the areas served by hospitals.
Hospital-operator surgeons had lower geometric and arithmetic mean payments.
Professionalgroup employment within a hospital system differs from investment in a physician practice or its MSO.
Quorum's fund ownership following restructuring also differs from a conventional practice buyout.
Pooling practice/MSO surgeons with lower-payment hospital-operator surgeons reduced the overall contrast.
Reporting the groups separately shows how payment levels differ by type of professional connection.
Prior studies illustrate why payment levels and acquisition-related changes require separate interpretation.

Nie et al. found that urologists later affiliated with PE had higher Medicare payments and patient volume before acquisition. [8] Dongre et al. similarly reported greater procedure volume before investment in otolaryngology, alongside higher payments per procedure after acquisition. [5] The higher preinvestment payment levels among our longitudinally eligible practice/MSO surgeons are consistent with the possibility that investorlinked cohorts differ before organizational investment.
text.formatted: Nie et al. found that urologists later affiliated with PE had higher Medicare payments and patient volume before acquisition. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[8]</ref> Dongre et al. similarly reported greater procedure volume before investment in otolaryngology, alongside higher payments per procedure after acquisition. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[5]</ref> The higher preinvestment payment levels among our longitudinally eligible practice/MSO surgeons are consistent with the possibility that investorlinked cohorts differ before organizational investment.

text.text: They do not establish that selection is the sole explanation, particularly because historical practice membership was not systematically confirmed at the investment date.
Other outcomes also vary across studies.

Singh et al. used commercial claims and a matched difference-in-differences design across procedural specialties, finding increases in spending and utilization after acquisition. [11] Braun et al. used Medicare claims in ophthalmology and found little or no overall change in total spending or use, alongside changes in selected clinician and treatment measures. [2] Annual total payment, payment per procedure, and spending per beneficiary capture different dimensions of practice.
text.formatted: Singh et al. used commercial claims and a matched difference-in-differences design across procedural specialties, finding increases in spending and utilization after acquisition. <ref type="bibr">[11] Braun et al. used</ref> Medicare claims in ophthalmology and found little or no overall change in total spending or use, alongside changes in selected clinician and treatment measures. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[2]</ref> Annual total payment, payment per procedure, and spending per beneficiary capture different dimensions of practice.

text.text: Annual Medicare payments summarize one reimbursed component of a surgeon's professional activity.
Higher payments can reflect a larger beneficiary population or more services per beneficiary.
Totals also vary with service mix and payment adjustments.
They do not directly measure personal income or practice profit and cannot establish the quality of care.

Neurosurgical Medicare research has shown that practice volume and service composition are relevant to payment variation. [9] Here, beneficiary counts were numerically close in the stateyear standardized comparison, while service units were higher among connected surgeons.
text.formatted: Neurosurgical Medicare research has shown that practice volume and service composition are relevant to payment variation. <ref type="bibr">[9]</ref> Here, beneficiary counts were numerically close in the stateyear standardized comparison, while service units were higher among connected surgeons.

text.text: Beneficiary counts and service units help interpret overall payment levels, although the provider summaries do not identify specific procedures or explain why payments differed.
Practice/MSO surgeons had lower mean claims-based risk scores despite higher mean beneficiary age.

One hypothesis is that a greater share of their care involves lower-risk candidates for elective procedures, including spine surgery, for which frailty is relevant to perioperative outcomes. [12] CMS risk scores summarize expected spending. [4] They do not measure operative fitness.
text.formatted: One hypothesis is that a greater share of their care involves lower-risk candidates for elective procedures, including spine surgery, for which frailty is relevant to perioperative outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[12]</ref> CMS risk scores summarize expected spending. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[4]</ref> They do not measure operative fitness.

text.text: These provider summaries do not establish surgical indication or urgency, so the elective-care explanation remains untested.
Age/risk balancing attenuated the practice/MSO comparison on both scales.
On the same annualrecord scale, the geometric mean ratio decreased from 1.31 to 1.25, leaving a point estimate near 25% higher payments.
The balanced ratio interval had a lower bound close to, but above, unity; the dollar CI crossed zero.
Concentrated comparison weights also limit precision: the largest weight was 10.2 times its base weight, and the annual-record weight concentration measure was 773.
Balancing addresses observed provider-level covariate means and state-year composition, while residual differences in procedure mix, referral patterns, and coding may remain.
The longitudinal analysis described payment trajectories around organizational investment among subsequently documented affiliates.
Both scales were imprecise, and omitting one highbilling surgeon reversed the dollar estimate.
Practice/MSO preperiod uncertainty does not establish parallel trends.
The hospital-operator preperiod coefficient provides evidence against that assumption.
Same-state and same-ZIP Medicare records do not verify continuous employment at the practice.
Historical affiliation dates are needed to interpret these models as acquisition effects on a defined practice cohort.
Public records may miss or misclassify investment connections.
Unmeasured differences in subspecialty and practice setting may also influence payments, as may referral patterns.
Connected surgeons contributed an index year, whereas comparison surgeons contributed averages over eligible years.
Cross-sectional inference and bootstrap intervals assumed independent physicians and did not account for organizational clustering.
Age/risk balancing used contemporaneous provider averages and does not provide patient-level adjustment for operative indication or disease severity.

The supporting longitudinal analysis used organizational investment timing without systematic confirmation of individual membership at that date and included only 14 practice/MSO and three hospital-operator parent clusters.
Medicare fee-forservice payments capture part of practice activity and do not measure compensation or patient outcomes.
Multiple comparisons were evaluated without multiplicity adjustment.
These descriptive observational comparisons do not establish acquisition effects or payment equivalence.
Documented PE-backed practice or practice-linked MSO connections were associated with higher unadjusted Medicare professional payment levels among US neurosurgeons.
The age/riskbalanced point estimate remained approximately 25% higher, with a lower confidence bound close to unity.
Hospital-operator payments were lower.
Longitudinal estimates remained imprecise and sensitive to influential observations.
